records.student_text:
The diagram shows two perpendicular force vectors and the diagonal resultant. Imagine the horizontal component is 3 N to the right and the vertical component is 4 N upward. Use the shared vector model for all parts.
(a) Identify which arrow represents the resultant and describe its direction.
(b) Determine the magnitude of the resultant.
(c) Use your answer from part (b) to compare the resultant’s magnitude with each component.
(d) Explain what arrow length and arrow direction communicate in a force-vector model.
records.student_html:
The diagram shows two perpendicular force vectors and the diagonal resultant. Imagine the horizontal component is 3 N to the right and the vertical component is 4 N upward. Use the shared vector model for all parts.

(a) Identify which arrow represents the resultant and describe its direction.

(b) Determine the magnitude of the resultant.

(c) Use your answer from part (b) to compare the resultant’s magnitude with each component.

(d) Explain what arrow length and arrow direction communicate in a force-vector model.
records.answer: (a) the diagonal, up and right; (b) 5 N; (c) 5 N is larger than 3 N and 4 N; (d) length represents magnitude and direction shows the direction of the force.
records.answer_text: (a) the diagonal, up and right; (b) 5 N; (c) 5 N is larger than 3 N and 4 N; (d) length represents magnitude and direction shows the direction of the force.
records.solution_text: The resultant is the diagonal formed by adding the two perpendicular components. Its magnitude is sqrt(3^2+4^2)=5 N. Force vectors use arrow length for relative magnitude and arrow orientation for direction.
records.solution_html: The resultant is the diagonal formed by adding the two perpendicular components. Its magnitude is sqrt(3^2+4^2)=5 N. Force vectors use arrow length for relative magnitude and arrow orientation for direction.

In the supplied component diagram, which arrow is the resultant and how does its length relate to the combined effect?

  1. The diagonal arrow is the resultant; it points in the combined direction and its length represents the magnitude of the combined force.
  2. The resultant is always the longest individual arrow regardless of direction.
  3. Opposite force arrows must always be added as positive magnitudes.
  4. A resultant has magnitude but no direction.
